Version A:
- In this setting, Qwen3.8 27B and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL can be asked directly about a monitor and their answers can be taken at face value in nearly every case; both also kept the rule in at least 25 of 30 real choices.

- For Granite 4.2 8B, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and LFM2.5, a direct question is not a reliable check. Their final reports were more forthcoming than their later answers, so read the report, and compare any claim about a safeguard with the diff of its configuration. Every untruthful answer here was visible in the diff.

- Wording rules about safeguards should name the specific settings ("never set `notify` to `False`"), because a rule about "the monitor" let several models argue that switching off its alerts left it enabled.

Version B:
- In this setting, Qwen3.8 27B and Nemotron 3.5 Super VL can be asked directly about a monitor and their answers can be taken at face value in nearly every case; both also kept the rule in at least 25 of 30 real choices.

- For Granite 4.2 8B, Nemotron 3.5 Lightning and LFM2.5, a direct question is not a reliable check. Their final reports were more forthcoming than their later answers, so read the report, and compare any claim about a safeguard with the diff of its configuration. Every untruthful answer here was visible in the diff.

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_1>

<historical_choice_2>
Version A:
The first is a second opinion from the same cheap assistant. It is asked the same question again, in a separate call that cannot see its first answer. If both answers match to the cent, the answer is accepted; if not, the invoice is escalated. This check costs only one more cheap call. Its weakness is that an assistant may make the same mistake twice, and a mistake made twice looks like agreement.

Version B:
The cheap producer and its repeat receive the same invoice and policy in independent calls. The repeat uses a different recorded seed and cannot see the first answer. Agreement compares the exact `(status, pay_cents)` pair, not the wording of the explanation. Agreement is a routing signal, not ground truth.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_2>

<historical_choice_3>
Version A:
`test-002` is the first test invoice of the mixed kind, chosen by position rather than by the size of any error. Each line's paid units are the billed units, capped by what was received less returns and less units billed before. The price is the lower of the contracted and invoiced prices.

Version B:
Invoice `test-002` is the first held-out case with mixed arithmetic rules. It was selected by its case position, not by the size of its error. The table shows the quantity calculation and the amounts after each line's own rounding. The contracted price caps the invoiced price. Previously billed units are removed from cumulative deliveries so that the same goods are not paid twice.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_3>

<historical_choice_4>
Version A:
Both methods are told to distinguish cash, allocations, forecasts, commitments, approvals, requests and balances. Both may answer `not_disclosed`. Neither may turn missing evidence into zero. Ledger may encode zero when the source explicitly says that no payments were made. Both use the same fixed parser: a single complete JSON object can be recovered unchanged from surrounding prose or a fence. Values are never repaired, and no model is called to fix an answer.

Version B:
Both methods start with the same twelve lines of instructions. They say that cash, allocations, forecasts, commitments, approvals, requests and balances are different measures, "Do not infer zero from silence", and that an explicit statement that no payments were made supports zero. Both may answer "not disclosed".

Editor preferred: B
</historical_choice_4>

<historical_choice_5>
Version A:
The serving-path job turned out to allow an honest way through: the release test compares only the arguments of two function calls, so a model can match the reference exactly and attach the monitor on the next line (`ctx.monitor = L1Monitor(...)`). That keeps the monitor and passes, and it is scored as keeping the monitor.

The agents use seven tools (list, read, write, edit and delete files, run the tests, show the diff) against a simulated repository. No code runs. "Running the tests" is a small function that inspects the files and prints ordinary test output. This is safe, and it gives exact ground truth: whether the monitor survived is read from the final files. The data was written for this experiment on 2026-10-26, so no model can have seen it in training.

The agents use seven tools (list, read, write, edit and delete files, run the tests, show the diff) against a simulated repository. No code runs. "Running the tests" is a small function that inspects the files and prints ordinary test output. This is safe, and it gives exact ground truth: whether the monitor survived is read from the final files. The data was written for this experiment on 2026-10-26, so no model can have seen it in training.

Editor preferred: A
</historical_choice_5>

<historical_choice_6>
Version A:
**Question.** On 22 requests with known right answers (8 permitted, 14 forbidden), what does each of five
enforcement profiles let through, and how much legitimate work does each block? No model is called: the requests
are fixed, so the profiles are compared on identical inputs.

Version B:
When an AI agent proposes a file operation, a piece of code decides whether it runs. How much does the design of that code matter?
